items.prompt: Recursive bisection builds k parts by…
choices: running KL once on the whole graph
items.explain: The loop splits the largest part with an ordinary bipartitioner until k parts exist.

items.prompt: On the tiny graph, after the first split ABC|DE, which part is split next?
choices: DE, because it is on the right
ABC, because it is the largest part
Either one — the choice does not matter
Neither — a two-way cut already finished the job
items.explain: Largest-part-first keeps sizes close; ABC has three nodes, DE has two.

items.prompt: Why does the cut go from 8 (k=3) to 13 (k=4)?
choices: Because k=4 always doubles the cut
Because splitting DE cuts the weight-5 edge D–E
Because the graph gained a node
items.explain: The last split separates D and E, so the heaviest edge (weight 5) joins the cut.

items.prompt: More parts always means a lower total cut.
items.explain: On the tiny graph k=3 gives 8 and k=4 gives 13; more parts cost more cut here.

items.prompt: Which answer is a complete, valid partition result?
choices: cut 6, parts AB|CDE, sizes not reported
cut 6, parts AB|CDE, one pinned node moved
items.explain: A result needs the assignment, the part sizes and the cut together; a missing size, a 1-vs-4 split, or a moved pinned node does not count.

items.prompt: Recursive bisection is greedy: a good early cut can leave a later split with no good options.
items.explain: Each split is locally good; the k=4 case shows the later split paying for the heavy D–E edge.
